{{Short description|Manifold of all orthonormal k-frames in n-dimensional Euclidean space}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Stiefel manifold''' <math>V_k(\R^n)</math> is the set of all [[orthonormal]] [[k-frame|''k''-frames]] in <math>\R^n.</math> That is, it is the set of ordered orthonormal ''k''-tuples of [[vector (mathematics)|vectors]] in <math>\R^n.</math> It is named after Swiss mathematician [[Eduard Stiefel]]. Likewise one can define the [[complex number|complex]] Stiefel manifold <math>V_k(\Complex^n)</math> of orthonormal ''k''-frames in <math>\Complex^n</math> and the [[quaternion]]ic Stiefel manifold <math>V_k(\mathbb{H}^n)</math> of orthonormal ''k''-frames in <math>\mathbb{H}^n</math>. More generally, the construction applies to any real, complex, or quaternionic [[inner product space]].

In some contexts, a non-[[compact space|compact]] Stiefel manifold is defined as the set of all [[linearly independent]] ''k''-frames in <math>\R^n, \Complex^n,</math> or <math>\mathbb{H}^n;</math> this is [[homotopy equivalent]] to the more restrictive definition, as the compact Stiefel manifold is a [[deformation retract]] of the non-compact one, by employing the [[Gram–Schmidt process]]. Statements about the non-compact form correspond to those for the compact form, replacing the [[orthogonal group]] (or [[unitary group|unitary]] or [[symplectic group|symplectic]] group) with the [[general linear group]].

==Topology==
Let <math>\mathbb{F}</math> stand for <math>\R,\Complex,</math> or <math>\mathbb{H}.</math> The Stiefel manifold <math>V_k(\mathbb F^n)</math> can be thought of as a set of ''n'' &times; ''k'' [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] by writing a ''k''-frame as a matrix of ''k'' [[column vector]]s in <math>\mathbb F^n.</math> The orthonormality condition is expressed by ''A''*''A'' = <math>I_k</math> where ''A''* denotes the [[conjugate transpose]] of ''A'' and <math> I_k</math> denotes the ''k'' &times; ''k'' [[identity matrix]]. We then have

:<math>V_k(\mathbb F^n) = \left\{A \in \mathbb F^{n\times k} : A^* A = I_k \right\}.</math>

The [[topology (structure)|topology]] on <math>V_k(\mathbb F^n)</math> is the [[subspace topology]] inherited from <math>\mathbb{F}^{n\times k}.</math> With this topology <math>V_k(\mathbb F^n)</math> is a [[compact space|compact]] [[manifold]] whose dimension is given by

:<math>\begin{align}
\dim V_k(\R^n) &= nk - \frac{1}{2}k(k+1) \\
\dim V_k(\Complex^n) &= 2nk - k^2 \\
\dim V_k(\mathbb{H}^n) &= 4nk - k(2k-1)
\end{align}</math>

==As a homogeneous space==
Each of the Stiefel manifolds <math>V_k(\mathbb F^n)</math> can be viewed as a [[homogeneous space]] for the [[Group action (mathematics)|action]] of a [[classical group]] in a natural manner.

Every orthogonal transformation of a ''k''-frame in <math>\R^n</math> results in another ''k''-frame, and any two ''k''-frames are related by some orthogonal transformation. In other words, the [[orthogonal group]] O(''n'') acts [[transitive action|transitively]] on <math>V_k(\R^n).</math> The [[stabilizer subgroup]] of a given frame is the subgroup isomorphic to O(''n''−''k'') which acts nontrivially on the [[orthogonal complement]] of the space spanned by that frame.

Likewise the [[unitary group]] U(''n'') acts transitively on <math>V_k(\Complex^n)</math> with stabilizer subgroup U(''n''−''k'') and the [[symplectic group]] Sp(''n'') acts transitively on <math>V_k(\mathbb{H}^n)</math> with stabilizer subgroup Sp(''n''−''k'').

In each case <math>V_k(\mathbb F^n)</math> can be viewed as a homogeneous space:

:<math>\begin{align}
V_k(\R^n) &\cong \mbox{O}(n)/\mbox{O}(n-k)\\
V_k(\Complex^n) &\cong \mbox{U}(n)/\mbox{U}(n-k)\\
V_k(\mathbb{H}^n) &\cong \mbox{Sp}(n)/\mbox{Sp}(n-k)
\end{align}</math>

When ''k'' = ''n'', the corresponding action is free so that the Stiefel manifold <math>V_n(\mathbb F^n)</math> is a [[principal homogeneous space]] for the corresponding classical group.

When ''k'' is strictly less than ''n'' then the [[special orthogonal group]] SO(''n'') also acts transitively on <math>V_k(\R^n)</math> with stabilizer subgroup isomorphic to SO(''n''−''k'') so that

:<math>V_k(\R^n) \cong \mbox{SO}(n)/\mbox{SO}(n-k)\qquad\mbox{for } k < n.</math>

The same holds for the action of the [[special unitary group]] on <math>V_k(\Complex^n)</math>

:<math>V_k(\Complex^n) \cong \mbox{SU}(n)/\mbox{SU}(n-k)\qquad\mbox{for } k < n.</math>

Thus for ''k'' ≤ ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1, the Stiefel manifold is a principal homogeneous space for the corresponding ''special'' classical group.

==Uniform measure==

The Stiefel manifold can be equipped with a [[uniform distribution (continuous)|uniform measure]], i.e. a [[Borel measure]] that is [[invariant measure|invariant]] under the action of the groups noted above. For example, <math>V_1(\R^2)</math> which is isomorphic to the unit circle in the Euclidean plane, has as its uniform measure the natural uniform measure ([[arc length]]) on the circle.  It is straightforward to sample this measure on <math>V_k(\mathbb F^n)</math> using Gaussian [[random matrix|random matrices]]: if <math>A\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times k}</math> is a random matrix with [[independent and identically distributed|independent entries identically distributed]] according to the [[standard normal distribution]] on <math>\mathbb{F}</math> and ''A''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''QR'' is the [[QR factorization]] of ''A'', then the matrices, <math>Q\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times k}, R\in\mathbb{F}^{k\times k}</math> are [[independent random variables]] and ''Q'' is distributed according to the uniform measure on <math>V_k(\mathbb F^n).</math> This result is a consequence of the [[Wishart distribution#Bartlett decomposition|Bartlett decomposition theorem]].<ref>{{cite book | last = Muirhead| first = Robb J. | title = Aspects of Multivariate Statistical Theory | publisher = John Wiley & Sons, Inc., New York| year = 1982 | pages = xix+673| isbn = 0-471-09442-0}}</ref>

==Special cases==

A 1-frame in <math>\mathbb{F}^n</math> is nothing but a unit vector, so the Stiefel manifold <math>V_1(\mathbb F^n)</math> is just the [[unit sphere]] in <math>\mathbb{F}^n.</math> Therefore:

:<math>\begin{align}
V_1(\R^n) &= S^{n-1}\\
V_1(\Complex^n) &= S^{2n-1}\\
V_1(\mathbb{H}^n) &= S^{4n-1}
\end{align}</math>

Given a 2-frame in <math>\R^n,</math> let the first vector define a point in ''S''<sup>''n''−1</sup> and the second a unit [[tangent vector]] to the sphere at that point. In this way, the Stiefel manifold <math>V_2(\R^n)</math> may be identified with the [[unit tangent bundle]] {{nowrap|to ''S''<sup>''n''−1</sup>.}}

When ''k'' = ''n'' or ''n''−1 we saw in the previous section that <math>V_k(\mathbb{F}^n)</math> is a principal homogeneous space, and therefore [[diffeomorphic]] to the corresponding classical group:

:<math>\begin{align}
V_{n-1}(\R^n) &\cong \mathrm{SO}(n)\\
V_{n-1}(\Complex^n) &\cong \mathrm{SU}(n)
\end{align}</math>

:<math>\begin{align}
V_{n}(\R^n) &\cong \mathrm O(n)\\
V_{n}(\Complex^n) &\cong \mathrm U(n)\\
V_{n}(\mathbb{H}^n) &\cong \mathrm{Sp}(n)
\end{align}</math>

==Functoriality==
Given an orthogonal inclusion between vector spaces <math>X \hookrightarrow Y,</math> the image of a set of ''k'' orthonormal vectors is orthonormal, so there is an induced closed inclusion of Stiefel manifolds, <math>V_k(X) \hookrightarrow V_k(Y),</math> and this is [[functorial]]. More subtly, given an ''n''-dimensional vector space ''X'', the [[dual basis]] construction gives a bijection between bases for ''X'' and bases for the dual space <math>X^*,</math> which is continuous, and thus yields a homeomorphism of top Stiefel manifolds <math>V_n(X) \stackrel{\sim}{\to} V_n(X^*).</math> This is also functorial for isomorphisms of vector spaces.

==As a principal bundle==
There is a natural projection

:<math>p : V_k(\mathbb F^n) \to G_k(\mathbb F^n)</math>

from the Stiefel manifold <math>V_k(\mathbb F^n)</math> to the [[Grassmannian]] of ''k''-planes in <math>\mathbb{F}^n</math> which sends a ''k''-frame to the [[linear subspace|subspace]] spanned by that frame. The [[fiber (mathematics)|fiber]] over a given point ''P'' in <math>G_k(\mathbb F^n)</math> is the set of all orthonormal ''k''-frames contained in the space ''P''.

This projection has the structure of a [[principal bundle|principal ''G''-bundle]] where ''G'' is the associated classical group of degree ''k''. Take the real case for concreteness. There is a natural right action of O(''k'') on <math>V_k(\R^n)</math> which rotates a ''k''-frame in the space it spans. This action is free but not transitive. The [[orbit (group theory)|orbit]]s of this action are precisely the orthonormal ''k''-frames spanning a given ''k''-dimensional subspace; that is, they are the fibers of the map ''p''. Similar arguments hold in the complex and quaternionic cases.

We then have a sequence of principal bundles:

:<math>\begin{align}
\mathrm O(k)   &\to V_k(\R^n) \to G_k(\R^n)\\
\mathrm U(k)   &\to V_k(\Complex^n) \to G_k(\Complex^n)\\
\mathrm{Sp}(k) &\to V_k(\mathbb{H}^n) \to G_k(\mathbb{H}^n)
\end{align}</math>

The [[vector bundle]]s [[associated bundle|associated]] to these principal bundles via the natural action of ''G'' on <math>\mathbb{F}^k</math> are just the [[tautological bundle]]s over the Grassmannians. In other words, the Stiefel manifold <math>V_k(\mathbb F^n)</math> is the orthogonal, unitary, or symplectic [[frame bundle]] associated to the tautological bundle on a Grassmannian.

When one passes to the <math>n\to \infty</math> limit, these bundles become the [[universal bundle]]s for the classical groups.

==Homotopy==
The Stiefel manifolds fit into a family of [[Serre fibration|fibrations]]:

:<math>V_{k-1}(\R^{n-1}) \to V_k(\R^n) \to S^{n-1},</math>

thus the first non-trivial [[homotopy group]] of the space <math>V_k(\R^n)</math> is in dimension ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''k''. Moreover,

:<math>\pi_{n-k} V_k(\R^n) \simeq \begin{cases} \Z & n-k>0 \text{ even or } k=1 \\ \Z_2 & n-k \text{ odd and } k>1 \text{ or }k=n\end{cases}</math>

This result is used in the obstruction-theoretic definition of [[Stiefel–Whitney class]]es.
